D.14 Theoretical Result

We first give the guarantee of our full-knowledge version (without cache size limitation).

Lemma D.31 (Formal version of Lemma 3.1).

Under the mild assumption, let kk denote any target size. If we greedily compute the attention score based on full information, then we can find the set Si{S}_{i} such that

f⁡(Si)≥(1−1/e)⋅(1−α)​𝗈𝗉𝗍i,\displaystyle f(S_{i})\geq(1-1/e)\cdot(1-\alpha)\mathsf{opt}_{i},

where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) are parameters.

Proof.

The proof follows from using Theorem D.17, Corollary D.18, Lemma D.29 with choosing θ=γ=α/(10​n)\theta=\gamma=\alpha/(10n). ∎

Next, we show the guarantee for our robust and approximate greedy eviction policy algorithm (Algorithm 2).

Theorem D.32 (Formal version of Theorem 4.4).

Under the mild assumption, let kk denote the budget of space limitation. If for each token, we greedily compute the attention score based on top-kk choice, then we can show the set S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} we generate each for token i∈[n]i\in[n] satisfy that

f⁡(S~i)≥(1−1/e)⋅(1−α)​𝗈𝗉𝗍i−β,\displaystyle f(\widetilde{S}_{i})\geq(1-1/e)\cdot(1-\alpha)\mathsf{opt}_{i}-\beta,

where α∈(0,1),β>0\alpha\in(0,1),\beta>0 are parameters.

Proof.

The proof follows from using Theorem D.17, Corollary D.18, Lemma D.30 with choosing ϵ0=β/(10​n)\epsilon_{0}=\beta/(10n) and θ=γ=α/(10​n)\theta=\gamma=\alpha/(10n). ∎

D.15 Extended Related Work for Theoretical Attention Problems

The static attention computation is asking the following question that given Q,K,V∈ℝn×dQ,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, the goal is to D−1​exp⁡(Q​K⊤)​VD^{-1}\exp(QK^{\top})V where D=diag⁡(exp⁡(Q​K⊤)​𝟏n)D=\diag(\exp(QK^{\top}){\bf 1}_{n}). [98] studied the static attention computation from both algorithm and hardness. On the positive, they provide an almost linear time algorithm to approximately compute the attention matrix. On the negative side, assuming a strong exponential time hypothesis (SETH), they prove a hardness result. Their hardness result is, unless SETH fails, there is no algorithm that runs in truly subquadratic time to approximately compute the attention matrix. Further, [100] considers the dynamic of attention computation problem. They also provide both algorithmic results and hardness results. In the work of [103], they consider the sparsification of attention matrix construction. In particular, they assume that situation that d≫nd\gg n, and show how to sparsify the columns of matrix QQ. [103] provides two algorithms, one is a randomized algorithm, and the other is a deterministic algorithm. Differential privacy is a famous and textbook topic in graduate school, recently the work of [101] shows how to give a differentially private algorithm for computing the attention matrix. For a given A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and vector b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, [104] formulates and studies exponential regression minx⁡‖exp⁡(A​x)−b‖2\min_{x}\|\exp(Ax)-b\|_{2}. Then [105] considers the normalization factor in exponential regression and defines the softmax regression problem minx⁡‖⟨exp⁡(A​x),𝟏n⟩−1​exp⁡(A​x)−b‖2\min_{x}\|\langle\exp(Ax),{\bf 1}_{n}\rangle^{-1}\exp(Ax)-b\|_{2}. [107] moves the scaling factor from exp⁡(A​x)\exp(Ax) to bb and defines a rescaled softmax regression problem minx⁡‖exp⁡(A​x)−⟨exp⁡(A​x),𝟏n⟩⋅b‖2\min_{x}\|\exp(Ax)-\langle\exp(Ax),{\bf 1}_{n}\rangle\cdot b\|_{2}.

D.16 Sparsity Preserving

Recall that in Figure 2, we observe that even when trained densely, the attention matrices of LLMs are over 95% sparse at inference time. Only 5% of the 𝖪𝖵⁡𝖼𝖺𝖼𝗁𝖾\kv\cache is sufficient for decoding the same output token at each generation step. Here, we provide some formal formulations for sparsity.

Definition D.33.

Suppose the following conditions

  • •

    Let S0⊂[m]S_{0}\subset[m].

  • •

    Let k=|S0|k=|S_{0}|.

  • •

    Let τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1) denote a threshold for truncating the value.

  • •

    Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) denote a fraction of mass (larger than τ\tau) outside S0S_{0}.

  • •

    Let mapping 𝒟:ℝd→ℝ≥0m{\cal D}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}.

  • •

    For each x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, 𝒟⁡(x)∈ℝm{\cal D}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is a vector that has length mm.

We say the distribution 𝒟{\cal D} is (α,τ,k)(\alpha,\tau,k)-good if the following conditions hold

  • •

    For all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, S0⊂suppτ⁡(𝒟⁡(x))S_{0}\subset\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x))

  • •

    For all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, |suppτ⁡(𝒟⁡(x))\S0|≤α⋅k|\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x))\backslash S_{0}|\leq\alpha\cdot k

Claim D.34.

Suppose we sample nn points {x1,x2,⋯,xn}⊂ℝd\{x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} from (α,τ,k)(\alpha,\tau,k)-good distribution uniformly at random, then we have

  • •

    S0⊆∩i∈[n]suppτ(xi)S_{0}\subseteq\cap_{i\in[n]}\supp_{\tau}(x_{i})

  • •

    |(∪i∈[n]suppτ(𝒟(x)))\S0|≤αkn|(\cup_{i\in[n]}\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x)))\backslash S_{0}|\leq\alpha kn

Proof.

Since for all i∈[n]i\in[n], we have S0⊆suppτ⁡(𝒟⁡(xi))S_{0}\subseteq\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x_{i})), thus

S0⊆∩i∈[n]suppτ(xi).\displaystyle S_{0}\subseteq\cap_{i\in[n]}\supp_{\tau}(x_{i}).

Therefore we proved the first property.

We know that for all i∈[n]i\in[n], we have |suppτ⁡(𝒟⁡(x))\S0|≤α​k​n|\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x))\backslash S_{0}|\leq\alpha kn. Thus

|(∪i∈[n]suppτ(𝒟(xi)))\S0|≤∑i=1n|suppτ(𝒟(xi)))\S0|≤n⋅αk\displaystyle|(\cup_{i\in[n]}\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x_{i})))\backslash S_{0}|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\supp_{\tau}({\cal D}(x_{i})))\backslash S_{0}|\leq n\cdot\alpha k

Therefore, we finish the proof for the second property. ∎

D.17 Definition of Loss Function

In this section, we follow the theoretical softmax regression literature [105] and define a number of functions to make the calculations of gradient and Hessian convenient. We also proposed a new penalty term (ℓ1\ell_{1} type sparsity penalty, see Definition D.41) into the final loss function, which is not studied in previous work [104, 105, 107, 110, 132, 133]. We first provide some function definitions.

Definition D.35 (Function uu, [105]).

Given matrix A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, let function u:ℝd→ℝnu:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} be defined as follows

u⁡(x):=exp⁡(A​x)\displaystyle u(x):=\exp(Ax)
Definition D.36 (Function α\alpha, see Definition 5.4 in [105] as an example).

We define u⁡(x)u(x) as Definition D.35. Then we define α:ℝd→ℝ\alpha:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as follows

α⁡(x):=⟨u⁡(x),𝟏n⟩\displaystyle\alpha(x):=\langle u(x),{\bf 1}_{n}\rangle
Definition D.37 (Function ff, see Definition 5.1 in [105] as an example).

Provided that the following conditions are true

  • •

    We define u⁡(x)u(x) as Definition D.35.

  • •

    We define α⁡(x)\alpha(x) as Definition D.36

Let function f:ℝd→ℝnf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} be defined as follows

f⁡(x):=α​(x)−1​u​(x).\displaystyle f(x):=\alpha(x)^{-1}u(x).
Definition D.38 (Function cc, see Definition 5.5 in [105] as an example).

Provided that the following conditions are true

  • •

    Given a vector b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  • •

    Let f⁡(x)f(x) be defined as Definition D.38.

Then, let function c:ℝd→ℝnc:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} defined as follows

  • •

    c⁡(x):=f⁡(x)−bc(x):=f(x)-b.

Definition D.39 (Loss function LexpL_{\exp}, see Definition 5.3 in [105] as an example).

We define Lexp:ℝd→ℝL_{\exp}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}

Lexp​(x):=0.5⋅‖c⁡(x)‖22.\displaystyle L_{\exp}(x):=0.5\cdot\|c(x)\|_{2}^{2}.
Definition D.40 (Loss function LregL_{\reg}).

Given A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

Let function Lreg:ℝd→ℝL_{\reg}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be defined as follows

Lreg​(x):=0.5⋅‖diag⁡(w)​A​x‖22\displaystyle L_{\reg}(x):=0.5\cdot\|\diag(w)Ax\|_{2}^{2}

We define a novel penalty function

Definition D.41 (Implicitly controlling the sparsity).

Given A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

We define

Lsparse​(x):=‖exp⁡(A​x)‖1.\displaystyle L_{\sparse}(x):=\|\exp(Ax)\|_{1}.

Then it is obvious that we have

Claim D.42.

Given A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. Let uu be defined as Definition D.35. Let α\alpha be defined as Definition D.36.

We have

  • •

    Lsparse​(x)=⟨exp⁡(A​x),𝟏n⟩L_{\sparse}(x)=\langle\exp(Ax),{\bf 1}_{n}\rangle

  • •

    Lsparse​(x)=⟨u⁡(x),𝟏n⟩L_{\sparse}(x)=\langle u(x),{\bf 1}_{n}\rangle

  • •

    Lsparse​(x)=α​(x)L_{\sparse}(x)=\alpha(x)

Proof.

The proof is trivially following from the definition of u⁡(x)u(x) (see Definition D.35) and α⁡(x)\alpha(x) (see Definition D.36). ∎

The final loss function can be defined as follows. Intuitively, we can write attention D−1​exp⁡(Q​K⊤)D^{-1}\exp(QK^{\top}) into nn subproblems where each subproblem can be viewed as one softmax problem.

Definition D.43.

If the following conditions hold

  • •

    We define LexpL_{\exp} as Definition D.39.

  • •

    We define LregL_{\reg} as Definition D.40.

  • •

    We define LsparseL_{\sparse} as Definition D.41.

Then we define LL function

L⁡(x):=Lexp​(x)+Lsparse​(x)+Lreg​(x).\displaystyle L(x):=L_{\exp}(x)+L_{\sparse}(x)+L_{\reg}(x).

Here, we compute the Hessian for several functions.

Lemma D.46 (Lemma 5.10 in [105]).

Provided that the following conditions are true

  • •

    We define α⁡(x)\alpha(x) as Definition D.36.

  • •

    For every i∈[d]i\in[d], let A∗,i∈ℝnA_{*,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the ii-th column of matrix AA.

  • •

    Let ∘\circ denote hadamard product.

Then, we have

  • •

    Part 1.

    d2​α​(x)d​xi2=⟨u⁡(x),A∗,i∘A∗,i⟩\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}\alpha(x)}{\mathrm{d}x_{i}^{2}}=\langle u(x),A_{*,i}\circ A_{*,i}\rangle
  • •

    Part 2.

    d2​α​(x)d​xi​d​xj=⟨u⁡(x),A∗,i∘A∗,j⟩\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}\alpha(x)}{\mathrm{d}x_{i}\mathrm{d}x_{j}}=\langle u(x),A_{*,i}\circ A_{*,j}\rangle
  • •

    Part 3.

    d2​α​(x)d​x2=A⊤​diag⁡(u⁡(x))​A\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}\alpha(x)}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}=A^{\top}\diag(u(x))A

D.20 Hessian is Positive Definite

It is well known that in literature [104, 105, 107], the Hessian HH of loss function can be written as A⊤​(B⁡(x)+W2)​AA^{\top}(B(x)+W^{2})A for some matrix function B⁡(x)∈ℝn×nB(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} (for example see explanation in Section 5.10 in [105]). In this section, we show that Hessian is positive definite.

Lemma D.47.

If the following conditions hold

  • •

    Given matrix A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

  • •

    We define Lsparse​(x)L_{\sparse}(x) as Definition D.41.

  • •

    We define Lsparse​(x)L_{\sparse}(x) Definition D.40.

  • •

    We define Lsparse​(x)L_{\sparse}(x) Definition D.39.

  • •

    Let L⁡(x)=Lexp​(x)+Lsparse​(x)+Lreg​(x)L(x)=L_{\exp}(x)+L_{\sparse}(x)+L_{\reg}(x).

  • •

    Let A⊤​(B⁡(x)+W2)​AA^{\top}(B(x)+W^{2})A be the Hessian of L⁡(x)L(x)

  • •

    Let W=diag⁡(w)∈ℝn×nW=\diag(w)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Let W2∈ℝn×nW^{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} denote the matrix that ii-th diagonal entry is wi,i2w_{i,i}^{2}.

  • •

    Let σmin​(A)\sigma_{\min}(A) denote the minimum singular value of AA.

  • •

    Let l>0l>0 denote a scalar.

Then, we have

  • •

    Part 1. If all i∈[n]i\in[n], wi2≥20+l/σmin​(A)2w_{i}^{2}\geq 20+l/\sigma_{\min}(A)^{2}, then

    d2​Ld​x2⪰l⋅Id\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}L}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}\succeq l\cdot I_{d}
  • •

    Part 2 If all i∈[n]i\in[n], wi2≥200⋅exp⁡(R2)+l/σmin​(A)2w_{i}^{2}\geq 200\cdot\exp(R^{2})+l/\sigma_{\min}(A)^{2}, then

    (1−1/10)⋅(B⁡(x)+W2)⪯W2⪯(1+1/10)⋅(B⁡(x)+W2)\displaystyle(1-1/10)\cdot(B(x)+W^{2})\preceq W^{2}\preceq(1+1/10)\cdot(B(x)+W^{2})
Proof.

The entire proof framework follows from [104, 105, 107], in the next few paragraphs, we mainly explain the difference.

The B⁡(x)B(x) based on LsparseL_{\sparse} is diag⁡(u⁡(x))\diag(u(x)). Note that it is obvious that

diag⁡(u⁡(x))⪰0.\displaystyle\diag(u(x))\succeq 0.

From the upper bound size, we know that

diag⁡(u⁡(x))⪯\displaystyle\diag(u(x))\preceq ‖u⁡(x)‖∞⋅In\displaystyle~\|u(x)\|_{\infty}\cdot I_{n}
⪯\displaystyle\preceq exp⁡(R2)\displaystyle~\exp(R^{2})

where the last step follows from Proof of Part 0 in Lemma 7.2 in [105].

To prove Part 1, following from [104, 105], we only use the lower bound of diag⁡(u⁡(x))\diag(u(x)). By putting things together, we get our results.

To prove Part 2, we follow from [107] and use both the upper bound and lower bound of diag⁡(u⁡(x))\diag(u(x)).

∎

D.21 Hessian is Lipschitz

In this section, we show Hessian is Lipschitz.

Lemma D.48.

If the following conditions hold

  • •

    Let H⁡(x)=A⊤​(B⁡(x)+W2)​AH(x)=A^{\top}(B(x)+W^{2})A denote the Hessian of LL.

Then, we have

  • •

    ‖H⁡(x)−H⁡(y)‖≤n2​exp⁡(40​R2)​‖x−y‖2\|H(x)-H(y)\|\leq n^{2}\exp(40R^{2})\|x-y\|_{2}

Proof.

The entire proof framework follows from [104, 105, 107], in the next few paragraphs, we mainly explain the difference.

Note that the B⁡(x)B(x) based on Lexp+LregL_{\exp}+L_{\reg} have been proved by [105]

We only need to prove B⁡(x)B(x) based on LsparseL_{\sparse} and add them together.

Note that B⁡(x)B(x) based on LsparseL_{\sparse} is in fact diag⁡(u⁡(x))\diag(u(x)).

Using Lemma 7.2 in [105], we know that

‖diag⁡(u⁡(x))−diag⁡(u⁡(y))‖≤\displaystyle\|\diag(u(x))-\diag(u(y))\|\leq ‖u⁡(x)−u⁡(y)‖2\displaystyle~\|u(x)-u(y)\|_{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​n​R​exp⁡(R2)​‖x−y‖2\displaystyle~2\sqrt{n}R\exp(R^{2})\|x-y\|_{2}

where the last step follows from Part 1 in Lemma 7.2 in [105].

Thus, putting things together, we complete the proof. ∎

D.22 Greedy Type Algorithm

In this section, we propose a greedy-type algorithm (based on the approximate Newton method) to solve the optimization problem.

Theorem D.49.

Given matrix A∈ℝn×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  • •

    We use x∗x^{*} to denote the optimal solution of

    minx∈ℝd⁡Lexp+Lsparse+Lreg\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}L_{\exp}+L_{\sparse}+L_{\reg}

    that

    • –

      g⁡(x∗)=𝟎dg(x^{*})={\bf 0}_{d}, where gg denotes the gradient function.

    • –

      ‖x∗‖2≤R\|x^{*}\|_{2}\leq R.

  • •

    Suppose that R≥10R\geq 10, M=exp⁡(Θ⁡(R2+log⁡n))M=\exp(\Theta(R^{2}+\log n)), and l>0l>0.

  • •

    Assume that ‖A‖≤R\|A\|\leq R. Here ‖A‖\|A\| denotes the spectral norm of matrix AA.

  • •

    Suppose that b≥𝟎nb\geq{\bf 0}_{n} and ‖b‖1≤1\|b\|_{1}\leq 1. Here 𝟎n{\bf 0}_{n} denotes a length-nn vector where all the entries are zeros. (Here b≥𝟎nb\geq{\bf 0}_{n} denotes bi≥0b_{i}\geq 0 for all i∈[n]i\in[n])

  • •

    Assume that wi2≥200⋅exp⁡(R2)+l/σmin​(A)2w_{i}^{2}\geq 200\cdot\exp(R^{2})+l/\sigma_{\min}(A)^{2} for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Here σmin​(A)\sigma_{\min}(A) denotes the smallest singular value of matrix AA.

  • •

    Let x0x_{0} denote an starting/initial point such that M​‖x0−x∗‖2≤0.1​lM\|x_{0}-x^{*}\|_{2}\leq 0.1l.

  • •

    We use to ϵ∈(0,0.1)\epsilon\in(0,0.1) represent our accuracy parameter.

  • •

    We use δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1) to represent failure probability.

There is a randomized algorithm that

  • •

    runs log⁡(‖x0−x∗‖2/ϵ)\log(\|x_{0}-x^{*}\|_{2}/\epsilon) iterations

  • •

    spend

    O⁡((nnz⁡(A)+dω)⋅poly⁡(log⁡(n/δ))CLOSE\displaystyle O((\nnz(A)+d^{\omega})\cdot\poly(\log(n/\delta))

    time per iteration,

    and finally outputs a vector x~∈ℝd\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

    Pr[∥x~−x∗∥2≤ϵ]≥1−δ.\displaystyle\Pr[\|\widetilde{x}-x^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon]\geq 1-\delta.
Proof.

The proof framework follows from approximate Newton (second order method) literature [134, 135, 136, 137, 138, 139, 140, 141, 104, 105, 107, 110, 111, 142, 143, 144, 145].

Following from Lemma D.47, we know the Hessian of the loss function is positive definite.

Following from Lemma D.48, we know the Hessian of LL is Lipschitz.

Following Section 9 in [105], by running Algorithm 4, we complete the proof.

∎

We remark that ω\omega denotes the exponent of matrix multiplication (i.e., nωn^{\omega} is the time of multiplying an n×nn\times n matrix with another n×nn\times n matrix). The most naive algorithm gives ω=3\omega=3. Currently, the state-of-the-art algorithm gives ω=2.373\omega=2.373.
